cards.headline: Bangladesh Bank doubles remittance limit for overseas medical treatment

pages.text: Bangladesh Bank (BB) has doubled the foreign exchange remittance limit for overseas medical treatment to US$30,000 from US$15,000. Under revised instructions issued by the central bank, authorized dealer (AD) banks can now release up to US$30,000, or its equivalent in other currencies, for medical treatment abroad without seeking prior approval from the central bank. The central bank stated these changes were introduced to provide greater flexibility in outward remittances and to facilitate legitimate current-account transactions under the existing current-account convertibility framework.

The central bank has also eased rules for outward remittances related to overseas education. Authorized dealer banks are now permitted to remit foreign exchange without prior central bank approval for secondary and higher secondary equivalent studies abroad, removing a previous requirement for approval regarding school-level education. This relaxation also extends to regular academic studies conducted through correspondence courses, as well as certification and professional courses. Additionally, the central bank has rationalized deposit requirements for Resident Foreign Currency Deposit (RFCD) accounts. Foreign currency brought into Bangladesh by resident Bangladeshis will only be eligible for credit to RFCD accounts if it is declared to the Customs Authority using Form FMJ, a Foreign Exchange Declaration Form issued by the central bank under section 8(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947.

cards.headline: More than 50,000 displaced by deadly Ethiopia border clashes

pages.text: More than 50,000 people have been displaced by deadly clashes in the Moyale area of Ethiopia, with many fleeing into Kenya. Displaced families are arriving in Kenya with little food or shelter, placing a strain on host communities that are already struggling to cope. In Moyale, Kenya, arrivals have reported brutal journeys, including women giving birth while fleeing and families arriving without bedding, cooking utensils, or food. Newborn babies have been reported sleeping on bare floors, and there are growing concerns regarding the spread of diarrhoea and the risk of malaria as mosquito populations increase.

Hawa Hassan, who fled her home in Ethiopia’s Moyale area, said her house was burned during the violence. She described tensions in the disputed border area regarding flag displays and recalled a 13-year-old girl being shot while sitting near a wall. Hassan stated the girl had not touched a flag, though her account of the killing could not be independently verified.

cards.headline: At least seven dead and more than 100 injured in Egypt train collision

pages.text: At least seven people have died and more than 100 have been injured after two trains collided near the Egyptian city of Giza. The collision caused several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment, according to the country's railway authority. The public prosecutor's office warned that the death toll could rise. One of the deceased was the driver of one of the trains, the ministry confirmed. Egypt's health minister, Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, stated that people are being treated for head injuries and broken bones. Local hospitals have been placed on heightened alert to manage a massive influx of patients. The Egyptian Red Crescent is providing psychological support and aid to victims and their families at the scene.

The accident occurred when a train traveling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, crashed into the rear of a stationary service heading south from Cairo to Aswan. Images from the scene showed overturned carriages and uninjured passengers and bystanders searching the wreckage for injured people. Following the crash, train services between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended while cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi ordered state authorities to investigate the circumstances of the accident and hold anyone found to have been negligent accountable.

cards.headline: South Africa's ANC records worst-ever local election results

pages.text: The African National Congress (ANC) has recorded its worst-ever result in South African local elections, more than three decades after the party of Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democratic rule. ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula described the results as “catastrophic.” While the ANC remains the country’s largest party, winning 31 percent of the vote, the results suggest a downward spiral amid long-held anger over corruption scandals and poor service delivery. The elections were held to choose local government councillors to run South Africa’s eight biggest cities, 44 district municipalities, and 205 local municipalities. The country is transitioning from an era of ANC electoral dominance toward a more competitive and fragmented multiparty political system.

The Democratic Alliance (DA), the ANC's main rival, won approximately 25 percent of the vote. The DA has sought to shed a historical reputation as a “white party,” a label it rejects, and stated that its modelling shows it won the votes of more than one million Black South Africans for the first time. The DA lost its status as the largest party in the economic hub of Johannesburg, the capital Pretoria, and the large Ekurhuleni municipality east of Johannesburg, but it retained control of Cape Town, South Africa’s second-biggest city. President Cyril Ramaphosa, who also serves as the president of the ANC, said political parties should approach upcoming negotiations to form coalitions for local rule with humility, stating, “Our people’s interest must not be drowned by the quest of political parties or representatives to settle political scores or petty squabbles.”

cards.headline: Supreme Court of Canada to hear challenge to federal firearms ban

pages.text: The Supreme Court of Canada is scheduled to hear legal arguments regarding the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of firearm models. The government maintains these firearms are fit only for the battlefield, while opponents argue the ban is unlawful. This legal challenge follows previous losses for opponents in both the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal. The ban, which the Liberal government has expanded to include more than 2,500 varieties of what it calls assault-style firearms, originally prohibited the use, sale, and importation of 1,500 models and variants in May 2020, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14.

The legal dispute centers on whether the Governor in Council—the federal cabinet—exceeded its delegated powers. A key question is whether the government adhered to a law that forbids using regulations to outlaw a firearm if it is deemed “reasonable for use in Canada for hunting or sporting purposes.” In October 2023, a Federal Court judge dismissed a request to strike down the ban, ruling it was not beyond the scope of the cabinet's powers. In April 2025, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected an appeal from a not-for-profit advocacy organization, firearm owners, businesses, hunters, and recreational and sport shooters, stating the initial ruling provided “thorough and persuasive” reasons. Writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, Court of Appeal Chief Justice Yves de Montigny stated he was not persuaded the government erred in considering public safety when assessing if the firearms were reasonable for hunting or sporting use.

The Supreme Court's decision will impact the status of prohibited firearms. While the government previously stated these firearms must be disposed of or deactivated by the end of an amnesty period on Oct. 30, that amnesty has been extended. The new deadline is set for 90 days after the Supreme Court delivers its decision. Gun control advocates have applauded the ban as a necessary step toward removing these firearms from circulation.

cards.headline: Netanyahu bloc reduced to minority in Israeli election results

pages.text: The Netanyahu bloc has been reduced to a minority of 53 members in the 120-member Knesset following the Israeli election. Anti-Netanyahu lawmakers hold 67 seats, while the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu holds 53 seats, which is five more than the anti-Netanyahu Jewish bloc. To form a government, a bloc requires the support of at least 61 members of the Knesset. Ilan Pappe, the Director of the European Center of Palestine Studies at the University of Exeter, suggests that Netanyahu may still form a government by enticing parties or lawmakers from the anti-Netanyahu bloc to join his, a tactic he has used many times in the past. Pappe notes that the results can be read in two ways: as a defeat for the Netanyahu government, or as a win for Netanyahu if the results are viewed through the prism of the apartheid nature of Israel. Pappe argues that the message of the vote is that violent Israeli policies within the region and occupied territory will continue.

cards.headline: Paraguay's Senate removes President Santiago Peña following Ueno Bank collapse

pages.text: The Senate of Paraguay impeached and removed President Santiago Peña over allegations linked to the collapse of Ueno Bank, according to reports from Asunción. Following his removal, Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as his successor. The political crisis escalated after the bank's services abruptly stopped working in the early hours of a morning, leaving millions of people unable to access funds for everyday transactions. The crisis led to the President being placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes. On November 6, 2026, protesters gathered outside the Congress building in Asunción to demonstrate the fallout of the collapse.

cards.headline: At least 34 people dead after migrant boat sinks off Senegal

pages.text: At least 34 people have died after a small wooden boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) citing an official source. The boat capsized while traveling toward Spain's Canary Islands, between the capital, Dakar, and the northern city of Saint-Louis. The Senegalese Interior ministry reported that one person has been rescued, but the number of people still missing has yet to be established. Saliou Diouf, founder of the Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all bodies recovered so far were Senegalese, though the nationalities of other people on board remain unconfirmed as search operations continue.

Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye expressed condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not to risk their lives on dangerous sea crossings. In a statement posted on X, Faye pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organizing these journeys, stating he would relentlessly fight those who organize the crossings and work to provide young people with reasons to hope in Senegal. This incident follows a November 6, 2026, interception by Senegalese authorities of another boat carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain. The Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, which it identified as the highest toll among the routes it monitors. Walking Borders estimates that approximately 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during that monitored period.

cards.headline: Annual number of children exposed to severe climate disasters rises nearly 50%, analysis finds

pages.text: An analysis by Save the Children shows that the number of children exposed to severe climate disasters each year rose nearly 50 percent over the past five years compared to the previous five-year period. Between January 2022 and September 2026, an average of 330 million children annually faced severe heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones, and extreme rainfall, according to the organization. This was an increase from an annual average of 222 million children in the earlier period. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, approximately 205 million children were exposed to severe climate events. Since 2022, 911 million children—about one in three worldwide—have experienced climate disasters of varying severity, representing a 17 percent increase over the preceding five years.

Save the Children stated that children are particularly vulnerable to extreme weather because their developing bodies are less able to withstand such conditions. Beyond immediate physical threats, climate disasters can disrupt health care and schooling, leading to long-term consequences. For example, wildfire smoke can contribute to respiratory illnesses like pneumonia, and school closures during heat waves can increase the risk of children, particularly girls, dropping out of school. In 2026, Western Europe had the highest proportion of children exposed to severe weather events, with one in two children affected following a succession of record-breaking heat waves. Meanwhile, East Asia and the Pacific have seen the largest number of children exposed to severe climate disasters, averaging 75 million children a year, or one in seven children in the region, since 2017.

cards.headline: 17 arrested and 55 charges laid in Ontario Provincial Police child sexual exploitation investigation

pages.text: Seventeen people are facing a total of 55 charges following a proactive child sexual exploitation investigation in Canada. The Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) identified the probe as Project Brace, an investigation targeting individuals suspected of making, possessing, and distributing child sexual abuse material. During the investigation, officers seized 424 electronic devices. While the probe did not directly identify any victims, the OPP stated that the investigation initiated 23 cases that remain active.

Project Brace involved the OPP and 15 other police services participating in a provincial strategy to protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation on the internet. OPP Det.-Staff Sgt. Tara Clark stated that online offenders use digital technologies—including social media, gaming platforms, messaging applications, and peer-to-peer networks—to use deceptive tactics to groom victims, distribute child sexual abuse material, and evade detection. Clark noted that combating these crimes requires collective action from law enforcement, families, communities, and industry partners.

cards.headline: Bangladesh Prime Minister announces six 100-bed hospitals for industrial workers

pages.text: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has announced plans to construct six specialized 100-bed hospitals in major industrial zones across Bangladesh to provide healthcare services for workers. The announcement was made during the first day of the fourth session of the Jatiya Sangsad, the country's parliament, while responding to an unscheduled point-of-order question from BNP lawmaker Advocate Shamsur Rahman Shimul Biswas. Deputy Speaker Barrister Kaiser Kamal presided over the sitting. The prime minister stated that the hospitals will provide medical services exclusively to workers and will be named to reflect their dedication to the workforce. The initial six locations for the hospitals are Tongi, Ashulia, Kaliakair, Narayanganj, Savar, and Chattogram.

cards.headline: Judo star Teddy Riner announces plan to run in France’s presidential election

pages.text: Five-time Olympic gold medalist Teddy Riner has announced plans to run in France’s presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron. Riner, 37, described himself as a candidate who is neither left-wing nor right-wing, stating he seeks to “bring people together” and provide “common sense, steadfastness, justice” to the country. Analysts have described the athlete as a long shot due to his lack of political experience and lack of party backing. He joins a crowded field of candidates ahead of the April-May ballot. Current polls suggest a hollowing out of the political center, with anti-immigrant National Rally leader Marine Le Pen appearing as a frontrunner and radical-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon trailing behind.

In a video posted on social media, Riner addressed potential criticisms regarding his background, noting he is not part of the political establishment and has never practiced politics. Born in the French Caribbean territory of Guadeloupe and raised in Paris, Riner used his judo career to frame his candidacy, stating, “Fighting has always been part of me. I know what it’s like to fight, fall and always get up.” He identified several national issues, including soaring debt, the rising cost of groceries, and the precarious futures of individuals lacking specific networks, family names, or skin colors.

Riner's announcement follows a period of personal and national tension. Approximately six weeks prior to the announcement, Riner faced racist abuse and online harassment after expressing anxiety on a television sports show regarding the rise of the far right in France. His entry into the race occurs as France experiences protests over the cost of living and ongoing protests by schoolchildren regarding crowded and crumbling classrooms.

cards.headline: Sudanese child refugees in Egypt face trauma and violence after fleeing civil war

pages.text: An estimated 400,000 Sudanese child refugees living in Egypt are experiencing profound trauma and poverty following three years of conflict in their home country, according to support workers. Clinical psychologist Rajia, who works with these children, says they have been pushed to a “violent” breaking point. Many of these children live in marginalized, unsafe neighborhoods in Cairo without residency papers or the mental healthcare required to treat their trauma, leaving them vulnerable to gangs, drugs, and a spiral of hopelessness.

Between 50% and 70% of these Sudanese child refugees remain out of school. Support workers note that cuts to humanitarian funding have left many children unattended while their parents work 10-hour shifts to cover basic food and rent costs. Social worker Tala, who works with war refugees, described the case of an eight-year-old boy who was suicidal and expressed a desire to die to join his father, who was killed in Sudan before the family fled to Egypt. Tala reported that the boy would become hysterical over small things and that his trauma and fear had turned to anger, leading him to seek ways to hurt himself and others. After several months of rapport-building, Tala helped the boy return to education.

cards.headline: Israel deports 14 foreign activists who supported Palestinian farmers in the West Bank

pages.text: Israel deported 14 foreign activists of American, Canadian, and European nationalities after they were detained while accompanying Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest season in the West Bank, according to an AFP report. The group of activists included a journalist and a 77-year-old activist. Israeli police also announced the arrest of three Palestinians who were accompanying the foreign solidarity activists. These deportations occurred approximately one week after 15 other foreign activists, including a journalist, were detained and deported. Israel’s Population and Immigration Authority stated the activists were deported for “breach of public order and violation of legal provisions.”

The Palestinian “Faz’a” campaign, which mobilizes local and foreign volunteers to support Palestinian farmers in reaching their land and protecting them from Israeli settler attacks, said the activists were assaulted before being detained. The Human Rights Defenders Fund, which provided legal support to the detainees, stated that the detention followed altercations with Israeli settlers. The accompaniment of farmers by foreign and local volunteers serves as a means of civil support and protection against settler attacks and difficulties in accessing agricultural land during the olive harvest season. During this season, American photographer Heidi Levine was seriously injured while covering settler attacks, AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh was beaten and taken to hospital, and a Reuters journalist was wounded in the leg by Israeli gunfire while covering an incident in the West Bank. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan cited figures indicating more than 3,000 attacks and violations were recorded during October alone.

cards.headline: African Union child rights body rules Ghana violated rights of girls barred from River Offin by taboo

pages.text: The African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC) ruled that Ghana violated the rights of schoolgirls who are barred by local custom from crossing the River Offin on Tuesdays and during their menstrual periods. In a decision adopted on October 20, 2026, during its 48th Ordinary Session in Maseru, Lesotho, the ACERWC held that Ghana failed to protect the girls from discrimination and harmful cultural practices. The committee has given Ghana 180 days to report on steps to build a permanent bridge and end the customary ban affecting the students. This case, Communication No. 0019/Com/001/2022, was filed in March 2022 by JoyNews Channel Manager and Ghanaian journalist Solomon Joojo Cobbinah, alongside the Banjul-based Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA), on behalf of the affected schoolgirls. Under a longstanding customary taboo rooted in traditional beliefs that defying the rule brings misfortune or death, women and girls are forbidden from crossing the river on Tuesdays and whenever they are menstruating. Because their villages lack local schools and a bridge, affected girls miss between seven and 12 school days every month, which the committee noted hurts their academic performance and places them behind male classmates.

The affected girls live in rural communities along the Ashanti Region side of the River Offin and must cross the river by canoe to attend school at Kyekyewere in the Upper Denkyira East Municipality of the Central Region. The ACERWC found Ghana in breach of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, specifically citing violations of the right to non-discrimination under Article 3, the right to education under Article 11, and the obligation to eliminate harmful social and cultural practices under Article 21. The panel ruled that governments cannot evade responsibility under international law simply because discriminatory restrictions originate from traditional authorities rather than state institutions once the state is aware children are being denied schooling. To remedy the violations, the ACERWC directed the Ghanaian government to expedite the construction of a permanent bridge across the River Offin and implement immediate, safe crossing arrangements so children can attend school uninterrupted. The committee also ordered remedial academic support, appropriate examination arrangements for affected pupils, policy reviews for underserved rural communities, and sensitisation programmes involving traditional leaders, educators, and families, alongside broader national efforts to tackle menstrual barriers to girls' education.

cards.headline: Office of the Registrar of Companies dissolves 323 companies in Ghana

pages.text: The Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC) dissolved 323 companies in Companies Bulletin Volume 49, exercising powers under Section 289(5) of the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992). These entities join thousands of silent businesses that have been struck off the corporate roll over the past four years in Ghana. While public commentary often attributes these dissolutions to a lack of discipline among founders who abandon statutory filings, an alternative perspective suggests the issues may stem from the transition between incorporation and tax compliance.

cards.headline: Canadian beach volleyball duo Humana-Paredes and Wilkerson secure 2028 Olympic berth

pages.text: Melissa Humana-Paredes and Brandie Wilkerson clinched an Olympic beach volleyball berth for Canada by defeating Americans Megan Kraft and Kelly Cheng in the women’s final at the NORCECA continental qualifier in Vega Baja, Puerto Rico. The Paris 2024 silver medallists won the match 21-16, 27-25 at the Areia Sports Complex to secure the lone direct women's NORCECA berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. While the quota spot belongs to Canada, the specific athletes who will compete are to be named through a national selection process.

During the second set, the Canadians required several match points to finish the marathon set. Brandie Wilkerson recorded a kill to bring the score to 26-25 before Megan Kraft and Kelly Cheng were unable to keep a serve from Melissa Humana-Paredes alive on the final point. Humana-Paredes told Volleyball Canada that securing a result of that magnitude during the Olympic qualification process and the current season feels incredible.

cards.headline: More than 100,000 sign petition for inquiry into UK role in Gaza

pages.text: More than 100,000 people have signed a petition on the UK Parliament website calling for a public inquiry into Britain’s alleged complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Reaching this number of signatures requires the British parliament to consider the topic for debate. The initiative demands an inquiry into any British involvement in Israeli operations in Gaza, specifically citing the sale, supply, or use of weapons, surveillance aircraft, and Royal Air Force bases. Signatories are seeking an inquiry with the power to question government ministers and officials involved in decision-making regarding the UK’s role in the war, particularly concerning the supply of arms to Israel.

The petition was launched by Jennifer Forbes, the chair of the executive committee of Your Party, a left-wing party led by former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn. Following the petition reaching the threshold, Corbyn stated on X that the group is seeking truth and justice. The UK is a longstanding ally of Israel and has reportedly supported the country's war on Gaza. A 2024 investigation by Al Jazeera reported that the UK provided military support by creating an air bridge vital to sustaining the intensity of the war, and that UK-based companies and factories supply crucial parts used in jets that bomb Gaza.

While the UK has supported Israel, experts suggest the country's policy toward Israel has shifted in recent months. After assuming leadership in July, Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that the ruling Labour Party “got wrong” its position on Israel and acknowledged that the stance caused “huge hurt.”

cards.headline: Forest-dependent communities in Bangladesh stage boat protest against Sundarbans pirates

pages.text: Forest-dependent people and local leaders staged a boat demonstration on the Kholpetua River in Gabura, Satkhira, on November 9, 2026, to demand the elimination of pirate gangs operating in the Sundarbans. Protesters urged the formation of a task force to launch operations against these groups and called for the intervention of the prime minister. The movement, which began on 28 October, has since spread across the wider coastal region. The Forest Pirate Eradication Committee has vowed to continue the movement until the Sundarbans is free of pirate groups.

Protesters alleged that forest-dependent communities have been left helpless, with most people unable to enter the forest to earn their livelihoods. They claimed that individuals are being forced to pay extortion money ranging from Tk50,000 to Tk1 lakh to separate pirate groups. Speakers at the gathering included Salauddin Liton, coordinator of the Forest Pirate Eradication Committee; Moniruzzaman, joint convener of the Satkhira district BNP; and Solaiman Kabir, president of the Shyamnagar upazila BNP.

cards.headline: More than 200 residents march in Asankragwa to advocate for climate change awareness

pages.text: More than 200 residents, including farmers, marched through the principal streets of Asankragwa in the Wassa Amenfi West District of Ghana's Western Region to raise awareness of climate change and its impact on farming communities. The march was led by Rikolto Ghana as part of its Community-Based Adaptation to Climate Change and Advocacy Project (CCAM), an initiative designed to strengthen farmers' resilience to climate shocks through community-driven interventions, income diversification, and improved local governance for climate adaptation. Participants carried placards highlighting effects such as biodiversity loss, declining agricultural productivity, irregular rainfall, flooding, and drought. The advocacy also drew attention to connections between illegal mining, environmental degradation, and climate vulnerability.

The march brought together participants from 10 project communities, including youth and women’s groups, traditional authorities, civil society organisations, and government institutions. Representatives from the Forestry Commission and the district’s Agriculture Directorate also participated. During the event, participants called for increased investment in forest restoration, sustainable cocoa production, agroforestry, climate-smart agriculture, and alternative livelihood opportunities to reduce pressure on natural resources. They also called for stronger forest protection and more responsible management of natural resources to protect the environment and the livelihoods of farming communities. Rikolto Ghana Project Officer Jonathan Owusu stated the advocacy aimed to promote environmental sustainability while improving local livelihoods and encouraging sustainable farming practices, particularly in cocoa-growing communities. Following the march, a stakeholder engagement session was held to showcase ongoing climate adaptation interventions and discuss partnership opportunities.

cards.headline: University of Ghana students protest 26 per cent hostel fee increase

pages.text: Students at the University of Ghana have begun a three-day protest against a 26 per cent increase in hostel fees. The demonstrators are demanding an immediate reversal of the fee increment and the abolition of the University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL)-managed hostel system. Protesters accused the university management of prioritizing financial considerations over student welfare and claimed the UGEL-managed arrangement exploits students while compromising their well-being. The students argue that the rising cost of accommodation, combined with what they described as deplorable conditions in some university hostels, has made campus living increasingly unbearable, especially for those from financially disadvantaged backgrounds.

The protesters contend that the 26 per cent increment will worsen financial difficulties for students already struggling to pay for tuition, feeding, transportation, and other essential academic expenses. They warned that rising accommodation charges could force some students out of school, particularly those who rely on affordable university housing to continue their education. The students described the UGEL-managed system as an arrangement designed to make money at their expense, arguing it places an excessive financial burden on students without providing corresponding improvements to the quality of facilities. They stated that the current situation raises questions regarding the university's commitment to providing decent and affordable accommodation.

cards.headline: Dhaka University maintains admission schedule despite University Grants Commission call to delay

pages.text: The University of Dhaka has decided to proceed with its admission process as scheduled, rejecting a call from the University Grants Commission (UGC) to reconsider test dates for the convenience of students. The UGC had urged universities with announced admission dates to adjust their schedules in the national interest, suggesting that public universities begin accepting applications in January with tests held in February. However, Dhaka University will maintain its deadline of 25 November for applications, with admission tests beginning on 5 December. This decision follows an emergency meeting of the university’s general admission committee. Dhaka University Pro-Vice-Chancellor Professor Mohammad Almujaddade Alfasane told Prothom Alo that the university had fallen behind schedule due to disruptions caused by the Covid-19 pandemic and that delaying the process by another two to three months could create another session jam. While the university is maintaining its schedule, students whose results change following the re-scrutiny and re-evaluation of examination papers—with revised results due to be published on 23 November—will be allowed to apply.

The decision to maintain the schedule means students who pass the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) supplementary examinations will not be eligible to sit for Dhaka University admission tests. The supplementary examinations, which are being introduced for the first time, are scheduled to begin on 1 December, while the university's application process closes at the end of November. Education authorities introduced these supplementary exams for candidates who failed in a maximum of two subjects in HSC and equivalent examinations to allow them to seek admission to higher education institutions in the next academic year. The results of the HSC and equivalent examinations were published on 31 October. Of the 12,40,798 candidates who appeared under 11 education boards, 646,685 passed. A total of 422,905 candidates failed in one or two subjects, consisting of 298,040 who failed in one subject and 124,865 who failed in two subjects. While examination results are routinely subject to re-scrutiny, questions have arisen regarding the effectiveness of the new supplementary examination initiative.

Other academic deadlines in Bangladesh include the MBBS and BDS admission tests for medical colleges, which are scheduled for 18 December. Applications for first-year undergraduate admission for the 2026–27 academic session at Dhaka University and Rajshahi University are set to close this November. Additionally, the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) and Jagannath University will also begin accepting applications.

cards.headline: Institute of Economic Affairs backs Ghana’s bid for BRICS partner-country status

pages.text: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) has welcomed Ghana’s decision to pursue partner-country status in BRICS, stating the move could broaden the nation's international economic relationships, attract investment, and open new markets for local businesses. In a statement issued on November 9, 2026, the IEA noted that the decision, which has received Cabinet approval, aligns with Ghana’s foreign policy principle of positive neutrality and non-alignment. This principle allows the country to engage with various global powers without taking sides in geopolitical conflicts. The IEA argued that closer engagement with the BRICS bloc would strengthen economic and diplomatic ties with emerging economies without undermining existing relationships with the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, the International Monetary Fund, and the World Bank.

The BRICS bloc represents a group of emerging economies with a combined population of more than 3.5 billion people and approximately 30 per cent of global economic output. The IEA suggested that this scale could offer Ghana significant opportunities to expand trade and market access. To maximize these benefits, the Institute encouraged the government to explore local currency settlement arrangements with member economies. Such arrangements would allow for trade using local currencies rather than relying solely on major global currencies, potentially reducing foreign exchange conversion costs and exposure to exchange-rate fluctuations. However, the IEA cautioned that realizing these advantages would require deliberate policy measures, stronger export competitiveness, and effective support systems to help Ghanaian businesses utilize the new opportunities. The Institute emphasized that the partnership should complement, rather than replace, Ghana’s traditional international relationships.

cards.headline: Illegal mining resumes along Tano River and Samereboi airstrip in Ghana's Western Region

pages.text: Illegal mining activities, known locally as galamsey, have resumed along the Tano River and near the main airstrip at Samereboi in the Western Region, barely four months after devastating floods submerged parts of the town. Drone footage captured by JoyNews journalist Erastus Asare Donkor and his team shows several excavators operating along the river and within previously mined areas, raising concerns about the risk of another flooding incident. The renewed activities are allegedly backed by influential individuals and could further obstruct natural waterways, exposing the community to another disaster.

Four months ago, floodwaters submerged almost half of Samereboi, including a water pumping station operated by SARMATEX to supply the community. While residents hold differing opinions on the cause of the disaster, some attribute the flooding to the anger of river gods over the failure to perform annual traditional rituals, while others blame illegal mining activities along the Tano and Samire rivers. Findings from a fact-finding exercise by local experts suggest that illegal mining at Kyemiso obstructed a critical water flow path connecting the two rivers, causing water to flow back towards the town.

The resumed mining operations are not limited to the riverbanks. JoyNews counted more than seven excavators actively mining around the main airstrip, close to the Samereboi township. These operations have left behind extensive pits and gullies stretching across parts of the airstrip, with some advancing towards the town and the banks of the river. The scale of these activities has raised questions regarding the effectiveness of efforts to prevent a recurrence of flooding and whether relevant authorities are aware of the renewed illegal mining.

cards.headline: Toronto developer accused of illegal tree removal and using allegedly fraudulent permits

pages.text: Toronto developer Modcity is facing new accusations of illegal tree removal and the use of allegedly fraudulent tree removal permits at a residential property in the Long Branch neighbourhood of Etobicoke. Four trees have been cut down without permits at a property connected to the company. As of early September, the city had 10 open investigations related to Modcity, which has faced numerous similar accusations in the past.

cards.headline: Omaha man loses Medicaid coverage following kidney cancer diagnosis

pages.text: Eli McCreary, a 64-year-old resident of Omaha, Nebraska, was informed by a hospital that he had lost his Medicaid coverage shortly after being diagnosed with kidney cancer. A hospital run by CHI Health told McCreary that his appointments would be canceled unless he paid out-of-pocket because he was no longer insured under the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities. According to documents reviewed by KFF Health News, McCreary was discharged from a substance use treatment program in March and was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney in June. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

After receiving notice of his loss of coverage, McCreary contacted a call center for assistance. A representative told him that his Medicaid benefits now required him to have a job and that he had not fulfilled the necessary work requirement to stay on the program. McCreary, who said he has battled drug addiction for decades, questioned the requirement, stating that his physical condition makes it difficult to find work. He told the representative, 'I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?'

cards.headline: Conservationists hope bespoke sanctuary will aid critically endangered Leadbeater’s possums in Victoria

pages.text: Conservationists are hoping a bespoke sanctuary will help the critically endangered Leadbeater’s possum population recover after only 13 of the lowland subspecies were left at the Yellingbo conservation area. Located approximately 50km east of Melbourne, Victoria, the Yellingbo area contains the last tiny remnant of the sedge-rich eucalyptus camphora swamp, a forest type that was once widespread in the state but is now nearly gone. This swampy forest also serves as core habitat for the helmeted honeyeater, Victoria's critically endangered bird emblem. The Leadbeater’s possum, Victoria's animal emblem, consists of two genetic groups: a highland subspecies and the smaller, more docile lowland possums found only at Yellingbo. While the species exists almost entirely within Victoria, a recent detection occurred over the New South Wales border in Kosciuszko National Park.

The Leadbeater’s possum is a small, soft, and nimble marsupial with gecko-toed feet that allows it to spring silently between branches at night. Dr. Dan Harley, a senior ecologist at Zoos Victoria who has worked with the species for decades, noted that they are not standard possums. The animals have exacting habitat requirements, preferring cool, wet, and dark forests characterized by large old trees for nesting and dense thickets of tea trees and paperbarks for cover. This specific habitat is vanishing due to the legacy of bushfires and state logging. At Yellingbo, the lowland possum population has faced a steep and ongoing decline.

cards.headline: Community members in rural Ethiopia continue using maternal health tools after pilot project funding ended

pages.text: Health extension worker Shitaye Husien and community volunteers Amanu Shuka and Aliye Feyiso are continuing to distribute recorded stories to families in a rural district of Ethiopia, one year after a pilot maternal health project concluded. Researchers from the Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs (CCP) returned to the area to observe the impact of the project after its funding stopped and found that local workers and volunteers had maintained the practice independently. The pilot, known as Supporting Health and Reproductive Equity (SHARE), was funded by the Gates Foundation and utilized social and behavior change (SBC) methods to improve maternal health outcomes. During the project, researchers recorded meaningful improvements in prenatal care visits, women giving birth in health facilities, and supportive behaviors from men.

cards.headline: Wildfires in Palangkaraya, Indonesia, create toxic haze and health crises for residents

pages.text: Wildfires engulfing the forests surrounding Palangkaraya, Indonesia, have besieged the city of approximately 300,000 residents with toxic haze for months. On the island of Borneo, the smoke has turned skies orange and created air quality so poor that residents must take extreme measures to breathe safely. Some residents use handheld devices to test for toxic particles, while others rely on visual cues from the orange skies or the physical sensation of an acrid smell and hacking coughs upon waking. To escape the smoke, some people are flocking to clean-air 'safe houses,' sealing windows with plastic sheeting, locking children in bedrooms, or using oxygen tanks in the evenings.

The air pollution has caused significant health struggles for local families, including Apri Dona Yusmelita. Yusmelita uses a nebuliser—a machine that transports medicine to the lungs—to help her five-month-old son, who has been sick for most of his life. Yusmelita reported that the infant suffers from a phlegmy cough that causes him to vomit, making it difficult for him to reach his target weight because he vomits what he drinks due to frequent coughing. Yusmelita also has a four-year-old child.

cards.headline: New poll shows Victorian Labor party trailing One Nation in primary vote

pages.text: A new opinion poll shows the Victorian Labor party trailing in third place behind One Nation and the Coalition, according to a DemosAU/PremierNational survey. The poll indicates Labor's primary vote share has fallen to 18%, an all-time low for the party. This figure represents a seven-point decrease from previous levels, placing Labor behind One Nation at 21% and the Coalition at 33% in primary votes. Meanwhile, the Greens' primary vote increased by three points since September to reach 17%.

Victorian Labor MPs have expressed both skepticism and serious concern regarding the results. During a press conference in South Melbourne, Ben Carroll refused to comment on whether he was worried about the poll. On a two-party preferred basis—a measure of support between the two most likely final candidates—the Coalition leads Labor 56-44, compared to a 52-48 lead in September. George Hasanakos, DemosAU’s head of research, stated that if these results were replicated on election night, many contests would be between the Liberals or Nationals and One Nation, potentially resulting in a “clear Coalition majority.” Hasanakos noted that because Labor and Greens preferences would likely flow to the Liberals, One Nation would need to poll very well to win in such a scenario.

The DemosAU/PremierNational poll included 1,562 respondents with an effective sample of 818 and a margin of error of 3.4%. Hasanakos stated he “double, triple, quadruple checked” the results of the poll, describing it as “extraordinary.” On election night, the Victorian Electoral Commission plans to conduct a two-candidate-preferred count (2CP). This process involves a count between the two candidates expected to finish with the most support after preferences are distributed. The commission selects indicative 2CPs for each seat based on polling, preference flow analysis, and previous election results, but it will not publish indicative 2CPs before election day to avoid influencing voter behavior.

cards.headline: Ancient societies in northern Peru remained generally peaceful despite El Niño flooding and ritual sacrifice

pages.text: A survey of the Lambayeque Valley in northern Peru suggests that interpersonal violence was extremely rare even during periods of ecological upheaval. Researchers examining the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project's skeletal record found that while mass ritual sacrifices were linked to catastrophic flooding caused by El Niño, widespread violence was not a common response to these climate events. This finding challenges the idea that resource scarcity driven by climate change inevitably leads to a rise in violence. Dr. Thomas Snyder of New York University, a co-author of the study in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, noted that very few cases of interpersonal violence were observed outside of ritualized contexts.

The research team analyzed skeletal records from 30 sites covering more than 3,000 years of the valley's history. Within this record, a total of 1,633 individuals had relatively clear dates of death, which allowed scientists to compare the timing of deaths with paleoclimatic modeling. Dr. Haagen Klaus of George Mason University, a co-author of the study, stated that the Lambayeque Valley experienced 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and long-term climate changes, but widespread violence was not among those adaptations. Klaus added that violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes.

cards.headline: Ancient underwater canyons in South Australia helped preserve early complex life

pages.text: Geologists have discovered evidence that dramatic sea-level changes carved massive underwater canyons in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia hundreds of millions of years ago. These canyons helped create the specific geological conditions required to preserve the Ediacara Member, a layer of Rawnsley Quartzite containing fossils of some of Earth's earliest complex, soft-bodied organisms. This research, published in Earth and Planetary Science Letters, provides new insight into the environmental changes surrounding the rise of the Ediacaran biota, which lived during the late Ediacaran Period approximately 635 to 538.8 million years ago. These organisms existed before the major explosion of animal diversity seen later in Earth's history. While the fossils are scientifically significant, researchers have previously debated how the landscape beneath these rocks formed and the specific role sea levels played in that development.

A research team led by Adelaide University, including geologist Karol Faehnrich and colleagues from the South Australian Museum, the University of California, and Pomona College, mapped geological features across the Flinders Ranges, including Nilpena Ediacara National Park. The team reconstructed the ancient landscape to investigate how sediments accumulated over time. They identified vast, southeast-oriented canyons that reached depths of up to 280 meters (919 feet) and widths of more than 6 kilometers (3.7 miles). The researchers believe these features were largely formed by underwater erosion that began when sea levels fell significantly, though they noted some may have also developed through erosion above sea level before becoming submerged. As sea levels subsequently rose, seawater flooded the landscape and sediments gradually filled the canyons, creating the environment that preserved the ancient life found in the Ediacara Member.

cards.headline: Fossil discovery in Colombia suggests major evolutionary transitions can occur without mass extinctions

pages.text: Researchers studying fossils from the Paja Formation in central Colombia have identified an ancient marine ecosystem where animal groups nearing extinction lived alongside newer groups that would eventually flourish. This discovery suggests that significant evolutionary shifts can take place without the widespread destruction typically associated with mass extinction events. Scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this pattern in an ecosystem containing a mixture of surviving Jurassic lineages and emerging Cretaceous groups.

Based on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a new concept called a “Biotic Inflection.” A Biotic Inflection is an evolutionary turning point characterized by the coexistence of older groups approaching extinction and newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify. The researchers believe an unusual combination of environmental conditions allowed this coexistence to occur, including warm greenhouse temperatures, elevated sea levels, and coastal waters rich in nutrients. Additionally, the emergence of new ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and the early Atlantic through the region that is now Colombia likely provided opportunities for different animal groups to thrive within the same ecosystem.

cards.headline: Machine learning reveals fish have gained schooling behavior 60 times and lost it 320 times

pages.text: Researchers have used new machine learning techniques to study how schooling behavior has evolved across thousands of fish species over the last 350 million years. The study, published Nov. 6 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that fish species have independently gained the capacity to move together as a unit some 60 times, while losing that capacity some 320 times across the evolutionary tree of life. This research is among the largest studies of the evolution of any behavior ever conducted in any group of species, according to the authors. Previously, studies of collective behaviors—such as fish schooling or birds flying in a flock—typically focused on only one or two species at a time, totaling a few dozen species. The new machine learning approach allowed scientists to quantify and study these behaviors at a large evolutionary scale for the first time.

cards.headline: JWST identifies more than 100 magnified stellar events in the Dragon galaxy

pages.text: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have identified 104 magnified stellar events in a galaxy known as the Dragon, located approximately 6.5 billion light-years away. This finding more than doubles the previous record of 44 such detections in the same galaxy. The study, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics in September, utilizes gravitational lensing to observe the galaxy's stellar population and potentially gain insights into the nature of dark matter. Because these magnified events reveal some of the most luminous stars, they provide a rare view of distant celestial bodies that would otherwise be difficult to study in such detail.

The magnification occurs through gravitational lensing, a phenomenon where the light from a distant object is stretched and magnified by the gravity of a massive foreground object. In this case, the light from the Dragon galaxy, at redshift 0.725, is being bent by a massive galaxy cluster called Abell 370. A portion of the Dragon galaxy is stretched into a shape known as the Dragon arc. The lensing effect is not uniform because the galaxy cluster is not a single, even mass; its gravity bends light by different amounts in different locations. Along specific lines called caustics, the light from the Dragon can be focused so strongly that its brightness increases dramatically. These distortions are created by the cluster's own stars and possibly dark matter.

cards.headline: Ancient Siberian tomb provides evidence of cannabis use from at least 2,800 years ago

pages.text: Researchers have found evidence suggesting humans have been using cannabis for its psychoactive effects for at least 2,800 years, according to a study published November 5 in the journal Science. The findings, which may offer the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use, stem from an excavation of the Tunnug 1 site in southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered nearly 1,500 whole or partial cannabis seeds and preserved human hair at the site, which allowed them to investigate whether the Scythians—a nomadic, horse-riding culture that occupied the Eurasian steppe from the ninth to the third century B.C.E.—were using the plant to get high.

cards.headline: Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives may lead to nutrient deficiencies, study suggests

pages.text: A study published in the September issue of the journal Lancet Planetary Health suggests that replacing standard dairy with vegan alternatives can lead to deficiencies in four vital nutrients. Researchers used computer simulations based on United Kingdom nutrition data to model how swapping regular milk, yogurt, and cheese for commercially available plant-based versions affects micronutrient intake. The study found that such swaps could result in deficiencies of iodine, calcium, riboflavin, and vitamin B12. To explore these potential public health implications, researchers utilized data from the U.K.’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey, which involved more than 3,500 people between the ages of 1.5 and 100 years old.

While plant-based milks and cheeses made from crops like soy, almond, oat, or rice are widely available and more environmentally friendly to produce than regular milk, they often lack certain nutrients found in dairy. The researchers noted that these risks could potentially be combated by mandating that nutrients be added to plant-based dairy alternatives and bread, a process known as fortification, which involves adding essential micronutrients to foods to improve their nutritional value.

cards.headline: Linear head motion may be more predictive of concussions than rotational motion

pages.text: New research from Stanford Medicine scientists and collaborators suggests that straight-line head motion, known as linear acceleration, is more predictive of concussions than the turning motion of the head, or rotational acceleration. This finding challenges nearly 85 years of scientific consensus that rotational motion is the primary driver of concussions. Concussions are essentially mild traumatic brain injuries, and an estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur every year in the U.S. alone. The study, led by bioengineering graduate student Jessica Towns, analyzed data from motion-sensing mouthguards worn by athletes across seven different sports. If confirmed by further studies, the results could influence safety guidelines and the design of sports helmets.

The study's findings contradict a long-standing theory in head injury biomechanics that dates back to World War II-era work by Scottish physicist A.H.S. That theory proposed that impacts causing the head to rotate—such as an uppercut to the chin in boxing—are particularly injurious because they cause shearing. Shearing occurs when the brain, a heavy and gelatinous organ, is stretched and strained as different parts of it rotate at different speeds. In contrast, linear acceleration tends to dominate when an impact force is directed at the head's center of mass. Examples of such impacts include a jab between the eyes in mixed martial arts, a lacrosse stick striking the side of the head, or a football player colliding with the top of the head while lowered or falling backward onto the ground. Jessica Towns noted that linear acceleration is not only predictive of concussion, but the threshold for what levels are considered unsafe is lower than previously thought. The study is scheduled to be published Nov. 9 in the Annals of Biomedical Engineering.
